item.title: Should Parents Genetically Enhance Their Children?
item.description:
Genetics

Should Parents Genetically Enhance Their Children?

If parents must pick the best possible child, should they also edit the genes?

Posted November 18, 2026

Imagine a world where everyone is healthy, intelligent, long-living, and happy. Intuitively, this seems wonderful, albeit unrealistic. However, recent scientific developments in genetic engineering, namely CRISPR-Cas, bring the question into public discourse: how the genetic enhancement of humans should be evaluated morally. This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

In 2001, when preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) and in vitro fertilisation (IVF) enabled parents to select from multiple embryos, Julian Savulescu introduced the principle of procreative beneficence (PPB), arguing that parents have obligations to choose the child expected to have the best life. In this post, I argue that accepting the PPB and the consequentialist principle (CP) that two acts with the same consequences are morally on par commits one to accepting the parental obligation to genetically enhance their prospective children—that is, embryos—a position Savulescu doesn’t explicitly endorse but I argue is committed to.

Savulescu, Sandberg, and Kahane jointly propose the following definition for human enhancement: “[a]ny change in the biology or psychology of a person which increases the chances of leading a good life in the relevant set of circumstances.” According to this welfarist definition, a conception of normality is not needed to define enhancement, as we do not define an enhancement as being better than normal, but simply being better full stop. Medical treatments are therefore just a form of enhancement. If a genetic alteration in an embryo is not expected to lead to a better life for that human, then it is simply not an enhancement.

Consequentialists are only concerned with outcomes; how these outcomes are achieved is morally irrelevant. Killing and letting die are thus ceteris paribus morally equivalent. To formulate my argument:

(1) Those who want to be parents have the obligation to select the child that is expected to have the best life, or at least as good a life as the others, based on the relevant available information (= the PPB).

(2) Application of the PPB leads to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without the application of the PPB, based on the relevant available information.

(3) If act A and act B have the same expected consequences, then they are morally on par. (= the CP)

(4) Genetic enhancements in embryos lead to the creation of children that are expected to have the best life or a life at least as good as without genetic enhancements, based on the relevant available information.

(5) Therefore, those who want to be parents have the obligation to genetically enhance embryos.

The ‘slippery slope’ is genuine.

Risks, High or Low

An objection often put forward is that genetic enhancements have risks that are too high or unknown and would make the life of the person targeted worse. However, when genetic alterations are expected to be more harmful than beneficial, they do not count as genetic enhancements and are therefore ruled out. Demanding a risk of zero to the targeted agents is over-demanding; otherwise, medical treatments would never be at the point they are today. In 2015, Chinese researchers released an article showing that the gene editing of human embryos is technologically possible.

Freedom

Still, many therapies and treatments in medicine are often deemed obligatory, even though there is no consent, for example, vaccination. Also, everyone should be familiar with parents sending their children to school, even though their children might not have given their consent. As a child, I certainly wondered who gave my parents my permission to do so. Just as education makes us more autonomous, genetically increased intelligence would serve the same purpose. Genetic enhancements aim to increase rather than limit one's possible choices in life.

Equality

There is a rather famous critic against genetic enhancements from Mehlman and Botkin, that is, being too expensive and therefore even when all parents follow their obligation, the children of rich parents will be far more enhanced or those of poor parents won’t get any enhancements at all. Concerning the worry of unequal access through wealth, Savulescu argues that this is not an objection to the PPB, hence genetic enhancements, but to all purchases of benefits like better education or healthcare. If equality matters, then these benefits should be available to all.

That is to say, those who accept the PPB and the CP must bite the bullet and accept that parents have the obligation to genetically enhance their embryos. As a consequentialist, Julian Savulescu should have no problem doing so.

item.title: Should I Let My Child Play Grand Theft Auto?
item.description:
Media

Should I Let My Child Play Grand Theft Auto?

How the video game affects people and what parents should know.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Grand Theft Auto VI has violent and sexual content parents may find objectionable.
  • The game is unlikely to psychologically harm players, but parents should proceed cautiously.
  • There are many questions parents should consider before deciding to let their children play.

Tomorrow, the biggest video game of all time will be released. The latest game in the blockbuster Grand Theft Auto series took 13 years and over a billion dollars to make. It’s predicted to be the biggest opening of any entertainment product in history.

The Grand Theft Auto games are an extremely violent, darkly satirical exploration of American culture. Currently, the game will only include a single-player story, but a multiplayer version is slated for release next year. I wrote previously about how to keep your kids safe while playing multiplayer games here.

It is unclear what content this game will include, as no one has discussed it publicly. If leaks are to be believed, the game will feature full nudity, including visible genitals and sex scenes. Based on previous entries, it will certainly feature drug use, offensive language including racial slurs, and frequent gun violence, including the ability to shoot police officers.

The game will absolutely not be meant for children. It is rated “M for Mature,” which means it is designed to be played only by people age 17 and older. However, many young people, especially high school boys, want to play it. I have worked with a number of young people who regularly play the previous game in the series, some of whom started as young as nine years old.

Some parents might decide to make an exception for their children, as they do with some R-rated movies. My parents let me watch some R-rated action movies like The Matrix as a young teenager, but they definitely would not have let me watch movies with explicit sexual content or graphic violence.

Parents understandably have questions about whether the game is appropriate and whether it will influence their children like the media suggests.

Will This Make Players Violent?

GTA games are extremely violent. I likely killed thousands of computer-controlled characters in the process of completing GTA V. They are not meant for children.

However, there is no evidence that the game, or any other violent media, will make players violent in the real world. The studies that purport to show a connection between violent video games and aggression often have serious methodological problems. Further, despite what the news media suggests, school shooters are actually less likely to enjoy violent video games than their peers. I wrote about this in more depth in a previous article.

Can Media Change Who We Are?

Although video games are unlikely to make children violent, there is some evidence that our opinions and values can be shaped by the media we consume.

For example, people who live in the Nadroga province of Fiji had traditionally viewed larger bodies as healthy and desirable. This began to change starting in 1995 when they started receiving outside television signals. Researchers surveyed a group of teen girls within a month of American television reaching their region and again three years later. Historically, dieting was rare in this area, and none of the girls reported vomiting to control their weight in 1995. But by the second survey, 69 percent of these same girls had started to diet, and 11 percent had begun intentionally vomiting to control their weight. That is, just three years of exposure to Western media seems to have fundamentally altered how the entire region viewed body image.

Importantly, GTA is not alone in featuring problematic elements. Each can be found in other movies, games, and even the news on TV. It is unlikely that this game will be the first time an older teenager hears racial slurs or sexual language, or sees nudity or violence. Most recent R-rated crime movies feature all of the above. Modern horror movies like Saw or Hereditary feature much more graphic violence than GTA does. Ultimately, this is why the series’ satire is relevant; the games are simply a more extreme version of the culture in which many of us have grown up.

It is therefore unlikely that simply playing this game will have more of an effect on its players’ values than their other daily cultural experiences. The aforementioned girls in Fiji, whose body image was drastically changed, were being exposed to a foreign culture they had not experienced before. American teens are already saturated with media showing extreme violence, sexuality, and crime.

However, people who consume more violent media tend to believe that the world is more dangerous than it really is. Researchers who have studied this “mean world syndrome” have found that people who consume more media are more likely to fear violence and trust others less. If playing this game drastically increases the amount of time an individual spends consuming media, it is possible that they will believe themselves to be in more danger in the real world than they did before playing.

How to Protect Younger Players

Parents who do not want their children to play this game should know that their children can simply download the game independently. Nearly all game consoles and computers now permit users to purchase the game digitally with a credit card or console-specific currency. To prevent this, concerned parents can set parental locks on game devices, including preventing purchases of games rated “M for Mature” (similar to blocking all R or NC-17 movies), or requiring a password before any digital purchases.

I also recommend that parents who are unsure whether their children should play such a game supervise their children or play along with them. As I wrote previously, this not only provides the opportunity to bond with children through their interests, but also lets parents talk about the game’s content and provide valuable context to what the children are experiencing. When the multiplayer version is eventually released, make sure that your kids are not chatting with strangers by turning off public chat.

Should I Let My Child Play?

Whether to let your children play a game like this is a personal decision. Reasonable parents can choose to ignore the recommended age if they understand the content of the game and believe their children are emotionally mature enough to consume it.

Below is a non-exhaustive list of questions parents should consider before purchasing the game for their children:

  1. Do I believe my child is mature enough to handle the game’s sexual content and will not emulate the problematic aspects of the sexuality they witness?
  2. Can my child emotionally manage seeing and perpetrating digital violence without becoming afraid?
  3. Are my child’s values strong enough to view characters acting immorally and not imitate them?
  4. Does my child have a history of substance-use issues that may be triggered by interacting with drug-related content?
  5. Do I trust that my child will talk to me about questions they have about the game’s content?
  6. Does my child understand that characters can be protagonists without being “good guys”? In other words, could my child watch Scarface without aspiring to be Tony Montana?

Conclusion

Grand Theft Auto VI will have a number of elements which most parents would find extremely objectionable. These are not likely to psychologically harm people who are mature enough to manage the subject matter and understand it in context.

However, the game’s content is highly inappropriate for most young people, and parents should proceed cautiously. If parents decide to buy it for their children, I recommend supervising them while playing and having open conversations about what their children are witnessing and experiencing.

item.title: Why We Get People Wrong
item.description:
Education

Why We Get People Wrong

What if our assumptions about human behaviour are holding us back?

Posted November 18, 2026

Two people with different opinions
Source: Getty Images, CreativeDesignArt

We get a lot of things wrong about one another. We often think we understand what other people think of us, and assume that the handful of actions we observe tells us something meaningful about their personality as a whole. Someone behaves rudely, and we conclude they are an unpleasant person. Someone struggles to find work, and we wonder whether they are trying hard enough. We interpret other people’s behaviour through our own experiences, expectations and beliefs, often with considerable confidence and remarkably little information1.

Psychologists have spent decades documenting the many ways our perceptions of others can be distorted; we are frequently wrong about others and even ourselves. These biases have consequences far beyond our interpersonal relationships. They shape whom we trust, whom we blame, what we believe people deserve and, ultimately, the institutions and policies we create and sustain.

Many of us feel we are living through unprecedented times. Particularly since 2020, rapid technological change, political polarisation and growing uncertainty about the future have made the world feel increasingly difficult to understand. But people have felt similarly at other points in history, and often with good reason.

A historical problem that sounds familiar

In nineteenth-century Britain, the Industrial Revolution was transforming almost every aspect of society. Population growth, industrialisation and urbanisation brought extraordinary economic opportunities alongside increasingly visible poverty, overcrowding and disease. Governments were faced with social problems on a scale that existing institutions were poorly equipped to manage.

One response was the Poor Law Amendment Act of 18342.

For centuries, responsibility for assisting people experiencing poverty had rested largely with local parishes. Someone who became ill, lost their employment or could no longer support their family might receive money, food or other assistance without having to leave their home. The system was inconsistent, often ungenerous and increasingly expensive, but it afforded local authorities some discretion to respond to individual circumstances.

The 1834 reforms sought to make poor relief more efficient, less costly and less attractive to those thought capable of supporting themselves. Administration was reorganised, and assistance was increasingly tied to entering a workhouse. Relief outside the workhouse continued in some circumstances, for the sick and elderly, but even then, many elderly and disabled people still ended up in the workhouse.

Oliver Asking for More; George Cruikshank, 1911
Source: George Cruikshank, Colour Illustrations, Charles Dickens, Oliver Twist, 1911.

Workhouses were deliberately designed to be places people would enter only out of desperation2. We are familiar with these institutions through Charles Dickens, whose Oliver Twist depicts a world in which poverty is often treated as a moral offence. Families were often separated, food really was gruel, and residents were subjected to arduous work and strict discipline. The severity was not an unfortunate consequence of inadequate resources but part of the intended deterrent.

The reasoning was straightforward enough: If assistance was too easy or readily available, people might become dependent upon it rather than seek employment. In fact, educating children was, in theory, supposed to be part of a workhouse remit, but in practice the standard varied considerably. Make assistance sufficiently unpleasant, and those capable of supporting themselves would presumably find a way to do so.

Of course, this reasoning depended on a particular understanding of why people were poor in the first place. A person unable to find employment, earning wages insufficient to support a family, or living with illness could not necessarily improve their circumstances through the threat of punishment. But policies built around assumptions about individual motivation often failed to account for precisely those conditions.

I don’t think the nineteenth-century reformers were simply cruel or stupid. They were attempting to manage substantial social and economic changes with the knowledge, institutions and political priorities available to them. Some were undoubtedly concerned with improving administration and reducing costs, while others had a more punitive understanding of poverty. The reforms also served the interests of those who wanted to reduce their contributions towards poor relief.

But the consequences illustrate something important: Our explanations of human behaviour influence the solutions we consider reasonable, even when those explanations are incomplete or mistaken.

What has changed, and what hasn’t?

Nearly two centuries later, we are living through another period of extraordinary transformation. Technology has changed how we work, communicate, form relationships and participate in society. Our scientific understanding of the world has expanded beyond anything nineteenth-century reformers could have imagined.

And, unlike our predecessors, we now possess the knowledge and technological capabilities to address many problems that once seemed insurmountable.

We have developed effective technologies that can substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions3. Advances in agriculture have enabled us to produce enough food globally to feed the world’s population, despite its extraordinary growth4. Vaccines, public health measures and medical research have given us tools to prevent and respond to devastating diseases.

But climate change continues, millions experience hunger, and preventable diseases still cause enormous suffering.

These problems are complex, and scientific and technological limitations remain. But increasingly, the question is not simply whether humanity possesses the knowledge or resources to improve people’s lives. The obstacles are frequently social, cultural, economic and political. They involve how resources are distributed, how institutions operate, whose interests they serve, and whether people can cooperate towards shared goals.

And underlying many of these obstacles are the explanations we give for why people believe and behave as they do.

Consider a more recent example of advocacy for punitive measures. Over several decades, psychiatrist James Gilligan studied violence in American prisons and sought to reform the way prisoners were treated5,6. In Massachusetts prisons, where violence, humiliation and abuse were commonplace, he developed reforms that emphasised treating prisoners with respect, providing psychological treatment and creating opportunities for education7.

Gilligan reported significant reductions in violence, and his research into prison education found extraordinarily low rates of reoffending among prisoners who completed college degrees. Even those regarded as among the most violent could, under different conditions, behave quite differently. But when William Weld became governor of Massachusetts in 1991, he opposed providing prisoners with free college education, arguing that people who couldn't afford university might start committing crimes just to get a degree in prison. His administration subsequently withdrew much of the state funding and undermined education delivery, despite reported drops in recidivism7,8. Sound familiar?

Neither understanding nor policy exists independently of the other. Our beliefs influence the systems we support, while those systems shape the circumstances and behaviours we subsequently observe. The resulting outcomes can then appear to confirm the assumptions that helped produce them—making the system self-reinforcing.

Institutions are also shaped by competing interests, and some people benefit considerably from arrangements that disadvantage others. Those with influence may understand perfectly well what a particular policy or economic incentive is likely to produce.

But the interests of a relatively small number of powerful actors can become difficult to challenge when much larger populations are persuaded that the existing arrangements serve their interests too, or that the problems those arrangements create are simply the fault of the individuals experiencing them.

This is where our understanding of one another becomes immensely consequential.

The way we explain another person’s circumstances influences how willing we are to help them, what we consider fair, and whether we recognise a problem as something that requires societal intervention. These explanations become part of our cultural understanding of how the world works, and help determine which institutions we defend and which we are prepared to change.

Why we get people wrong

This blog is about those explanations: How we come to understand other people’s behaviour, why we so often get it wrong, and what the consequences are for the societies we live in. I’ll draw on research across psychology, biology, anthropology, and the social sciences to explore how individual behaviour interacts with the environments in which it develops. Sometimes that will mean examining the assumptions we make about our friends, strangers and, most importantly, ourselves. At other times, it will mean considering how those same assumptions influence our attitudes towards responsibility, inequality, politics and the institutions that govern our lives.

Understanding these processes is only part of the task. If we want different outcomes, we also have to use that understanding to change the conditions that produce them.

The nineteenth-century workhouse offers one illustration of what can happen when our assumptions about human behaviour inform our attempts to solve social problems. Seeing the same way of thinking manifest centuries later, despite all our accumulated knowledge, tells us something important about the real barriers to solving our problems.

One of the great challenges of our time is learning how to use knowledge to build societies that work better for the people living within them.

Perhaps a useful place to begin is by examining how much we still get wrong about one another and ourselves.

item.title: The Family Table: Finding Your Place as an Elder
item.description:
Family Dynamics

The Family Table: Finding Your Place as an Elder

Holidays reveal how our place at the family table shifts across a lifetime.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Our place at the family table shifts over our lifetime.
  • Few parents are prepared for the changing role of having adult children.
  • Holiday tables change, and accepting this leaves room for new traditions and stories.
Source: hudsoncrafted/Pixabay

Note: This post may stir feelings of grief, estrangement, and old wounds. Not every family table was safe, and that distance or estrangement can be a valid, even necessary, choice.

The Idea of a Table

With the holidays approaching, many of us think about our actual family tables and where everyone will sit. The idea of a family table is also a metaphor for our relationships. For example: Who sets it? Who is served first? Who sits at the head? Who was not invited? Over the course of our lifetimes, our place at the table shifts and rearranges itself, often because of losses, marriages and divorces, grandchildren, aging siblings, distance, and the chosen family members who have pulled up a chair.

We begin our lives at the children’s table; then we are perhaps the chef and server; and as elders, we might be lucky enough to become guests at our children’s or chosen family’s tables.

Adult Children

Lately, many people in middle age and beyond have spoken about the changing dynamics of their relationships with their adult children. These feelings can be magnified during the holidays. Things are simply not what they used to be. When our children were young, their world revolved around us and our world revolved around them. Many of us have read books on parenting children and teenagers, but few of us were offered books or conversations about navigating life with our adult children. For many parents of adult children, there’s a deep ache in realizing that their role isn't what it used to be.

Role Shifts

We move from managing our children’s lives to being something of an outsider. We are no longer involved in their everyday activities, and sometimes we don’t even know what they’re up to. We might have taught our children the power of independence, and now there is a lot of holding on and letting go.

Becoming a mother-in-law is another challenging role shift. Sharing our children with spouses and in-law families is not always an easy transition, especially if the partner is different from what we imagined for our child and/or if the couple lives far away.

Another shift is that children might begin worrying about their parents rather than the other way around. Perhaps the parents have physical or psychological health problems that call for their children’s intervention and care. It’s important for elders to accept help while maintaining their dignity. At the same time, many elders are still caring for aging parents or grieving them.

Estrangement and distance

Sadly, estrangement has become increasingly common. Perhaps more common than people care to admit. Very often, because of shame, it’s carried in silence, which can be very painful.

One woman shared the story of organizing a holiday with her three adult children and four small grandchildren at a beautiful resort. One minute they were a happy family, and the next minute they were estranged. She still isn’t sure what happened, but on the last day of the trip, one of her adult children picked a fight about something that had happened years earlier, leaving the grandparents speechless. Everyone went home, and the adult child who picked a fight simply cut off contact and never really understood why.

Becoming a Grandparent

Those who were close with their grandparents understand how vitally important this relationship can be. I am the daughter of immigrants, and my parents worked very long hours to make ends meet, so my grandmother was my primary caretaker. Because I remember the closeness of that relationship, I was eager and excited to become a grandmother. I thought long and hard about what kind of grandmother I wanted to be and how I would handle certain situations.

One thing grandparents learn quickly is the importance of keeping their opinions to themselves. They realize this is important, especially if they want to keep the lines of communication open with their adult children. This can be difficult, especially when they reach a stage of life when they might have—at a stage of life when they may hold strong opinions that their children don’t want to hear. Many elders say that their children really don’t want their advice. The truth is, younger generations can find most of what they want online, especially now that AI has become an integral part of our lives. The challenge is knowing when to speak and when to stay quiet.

Thanksgiving and Holiday Tables

For those without children, with distant children, or whose friends have become their truest family, the holiday table might look different from what they imagined. Holidays remind us that change is always happening. Sometimes there are empty chairs at the table, sometimes new faces, and sometimes more than one table. Some people might choose new or different traditions, and change requires acceptance. Change calls for acceptance, which leaves room for something new. Remember, nobody ever promised that things would stay the same. Enjoy whatever gathering you're part of. There will always be new stories to tell.

item.title: When Psychiatry Becomes Mind-Blind
item.description:
Psychiatry

When Psychiatry Becomes Mind-Blind

Biologist Michael Levin's term examines stigma and psychiatric diagnosis.

Posted November 18, 2026

Key points
  • Mind-blindness is the failure to grasp the cognition of other beings.
  • A doctor who told me I'd be locked up for life was mind-blind.
  • Rather than "sick," hearing voices and even seeing things are common.
  • Carl Jung praised his visions as the source of his greatest ideas.

I once sat in a room while a psychiatrist discussed with my parents his belief that I would face a lifetime of institutionalization. At 15, I was perfectly capable of understanding him. The conversation excluded me not because I couldn’t grasp it but because that doctor had uttered the word “schizophrenia.” Once he did, the sense that anything real might exist in my head, even the most basic sense, evaporated.

The people around me became mind-blind.

I borrow this term from biologist and natural philosopher Michael Levin: Mind-blindness is the inability to recognize the minds of others. Michael was gracious enough to chat with me about it. He believes humans exist in a world full of minds, with cognition a potential not just for other creatures, but for cells, large language models, even algorithms.

“We tend to think of things as either dumb like rocks or smart like humans and angels,” Levin said. Instead, Levin believes that the sciences of cybernetics and the tools of behavior science now show mind exists on a continuum, involving testable traits like whether a being can learn and what its competencies are.

Mind-Blindness Begins With Other Humans

As Levin puts it, it’s more a question of what kind of intelligence exists, and how much, than a yes-or-no distinction.

When I told Michael Levin I believed humans’ mind-blindness begins with other humans, he said, “You’re absolutely right.” And he added, “I think the problem is a scarcity mentality with respect to compassion. It’s as if people thought, if we allow too many into the club of cognition, there will not be enough care or love for me.”

I once spoke in sign language with an orangutan named Chantek, who indicated he found his cage mate Sibu a bit messy. Remembering the thoughtfulness of his eyes still makes seeing a caged animal unbearable to me. I live with two cats who often let me know, with headbutts and meows, that I’m about to get sick before I know it; I know we overlook the capacities of the beings around us.

And humans can be highly mind-blind to each other.

White Europeans have historically demonstrated mind-blindness to other racial groups, to the point of enslaving them. Jeffrey Epstein was mind-blind to women, which no doubt made him feel better about his abuse. And based on their testimony, Lindsay Clancy’s caregivers remained mind-blind to the actual thoughts she was having. They slotted her pain into symptom categories, missing the awful acts her mind pushed her toward.

Psychiatry, and the culture that accepts its premises, has been mind-blind. This isn’t only true of my early doctor. Autistic people have suffered with the stigma that they lack “theory of mind,” or an understanding that the people around them have minds and feelings.

Bias and Discrimination

When I taught, fellow professors often shared their conviction that students who bothered them must be “on the spectrum.” Though “spectrum” has gotten to be a shorthand for a jumble of traits that don’t even fit together: insensitivity, oversensitivity, bluntness, shyness. These biases still lead to real discrimination, though they’re based largely on misunderstandings of subtle differences.

Then there is the child I was, turned to vapor by the word “schizophrenia.” My diagnosis changed ultimately. But I would be who I am with or without a word from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual next to my name.

Mental states, which DSM terms try and fail to pin down, are less hardwired, binary differences between people than they are part of the human condition, one piece of all our potential. They reflect inborn flaws less than they show the tumult of living a life in this human body.

A good share of the population—as many as 15 percent or more of adults—will at some point in their lives hear voices. Up to 38 percent will experience visual hallucinations, a high enough number to suggest this alone shouldn’t be enough to diagnose psychosis, though it very well could be. And one-quarter to one-third of people who have what is diagnosed as a full-blown schizophrenic episode will never have another one. Those whose conditions become chronic may be impaired as much or more by the treatment as the underlying mental state.

Trauma makes the experience of psychosis far more likely, certainly a factor for me as a girl. Difficult life experiences can also plant the seeds of creativity and novel thought. This was true of mind pioneer Carl Jung. An early exposure to death, and later sexual abuse, traumatized Jung, and as an adult he had an extended period of hallucinations.

Jung described “incessant visions” in his Red Book and compared their impact to thunderstorms and floods. Though this period wasn’t a pointless bout of “illness” in Jung’s life—he called that time the root of his most important ideas, such as the existence of archetypes and the collective unconscious.

Pathways to Care

Michael Levin has more to offer the field of psychiatry than the helpful idea of mind-blindness. He believes that in the future we might practice a somatic psychiatry that exploits bioelectricity, the “cognitive glue” aligning cells toward organ-scale anatomical goals, using bioelectrical signaling as an interface through which to communicate desired healthy form and function.

Levin also told me, “Our cells provide another level of intelligence in the body,” and communicating at these other levels might offer pathways to mind care.

Before we fully understand the many ways we can help ourselves, we need to drop narrow beliefs about minds.

Carl Jung wrote that our inner worlds are “truly infinite, in no way poorer than the outer one,” so powerful and individual that “humans live in two worlds.” We share the former world with a dizzying array of other beings. Perhaps, in ways that are not always easy to understand, we share the inner world as well.

“What I hope is that when we can acknowledge that the mind can belong to things that don’t look anything like us,” Michael Levin told me, “our differences become laughably small.”
